subject: Oncology and Hematology
vignette: A 70-year-old man has 4 months of fatigue, headache, blurred vision, and easy bruising. Examination shows pallor, lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory studies show anemia and an IgM concentration of 4800 mg/dL. Funduscopy shows dilated, segmented, and tortuous retinal veins.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Multiple myeloma
Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance
Chronic lymphocytic leukemia
Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia
Acute myelogenous leukemia

explanation_correct: Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia is defined by overproduction of IgM, the largest immunoglobulin, which raises serum viscosity. The classic picture includes anemia, constitutional B symptoms, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and hyperviscosity manifestations such as headache, bleeding, blurry vision, and ataxia. Marrow shows more than 10% lymphoplasmacytic cells with intranuclear IgM pseudoinclusions.

explanation_incorrect.A: Multiple myeloma overproduces IgG or IgA and causes lytic lesions and CRAB findings rather than IgM hyperviscosity and organomegaly.
explanation_incorrect.B: MGUS is asymptomatic, has an M spike below 3 g/dL, and does not cause hyperviscosity or lymphadenopathy.
explanation_incorrect.C: CLL is an indolent CD5+/CD20+/CD23+ B-cell neoplasm with smudge cells, not an IgM-secreting lymphoplasmacytic tumor.
explanation_incorrect.E: AML presents with circulating myeloblasts, Auer rods, and cytopenias, not with an IgM paraprotein and hyperviscosity.

educationalObjective: Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia produces IgM, causing hyperviscosity with headache, visual changes, bleeding, ataxia, and sausage-link retinal veins.

subject: Oncology and Hematology
vignette: A 64-year-old woman with Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia reports progressive headache, blurred vision, and unsteady gait. Serum viscosity is markedly elevated. Funduscopic examination shows dilated, segmented, and tortuous retinal veins described as a sausage-link appearance.
question: Which of the following best explains these neurologic and retinal findings?

options.text: Hyperviscosity from high-molecular-weight IgM impairing retinal and cerebral microcirculation
Hypertension-induced retinal arterial narrowing and vasospasm
Hypercalcemia-induced vascular calcification and encephalopathy
Direct leukemic infiltration of the retina and brain by lymphoblasts
Thrombotic microangiopathy from antiphospholipid antibodies

explanation_correct: IgM is the largest immunoglobulin and, at high concentrations, markedly increases serum viscosity. Sludging in the microcirculation produces headache, bleeding, blurry vision, and ataxia, and funduscopy shows the classic dilated, segmented, tortuous sausage-link retinal veins. Hyperviscosity symptoms are a defining clinical feature of Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia.

explanation_incorrect.B: Hypertensive retinopathy produces arterial narrowing, hemorrhages, and exudates rather than segmentally dilated tortuous veins.
explanation_incorrect.C: Hypercalcemia causes constipation, psychosis, and bone lesions; it is a myeloma feature and does not produce sausage-link retinal veins.
explanation_incorrect.D: Retinal and CNS leukemic infiltration occurs with high-blast acute leukemias, not with this indolent IgM-producing neoplasm.
explanation_incorrect.E: Antiphospholipid syndrome causes thrombotic events and thrombocytopenia, not the hyperviscosity syndrome described here.

educationalObjective: The large IgM molecule causes hyperviscosity in Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia, producing headache, bleeding, ataxia, and sausage-link retinal veins.

subject: Oncology and Hematology
vignette: A 67-year-old man has an IgM M spike, anemia, and hyperviscosity symptoms. Bone marrow aspirate shows an infiltrate of small lymphocytes with plasma cell features; many cells contain round intranuclear inclusions that stain positively for IgM.
question: Which of the following best characterizes the bone marrow findings in this disorder?

options.text: More than 10% monoclonal plasma cells with clock-face chromatin and intracytoplasmic inclusions
At least 20% myeloblasts with Auer rods
More than 10% monoclonal B lymphocytes with plasma cell features and intranuclear IgM pseudoinclusions
Fewer than 10% polytypic plasma cells without CRAB findings
Mature B cells with filamentous hairlike projections and marrow fibrosis

explanation_correct: The marrow in Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia shows more than 10% monoclonal B lymphocytes with plasma cell features, the picture of lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma. Intranuclear pseudoinclusions containing IgM are characteristic and contrast with the intracytoplasmic immunoglobulin inclusions and clock-face chromatin of myeloma plasma cells.

explanation_incorrect.A: Clock-face chromatin and intracytoplasmic immunoglobulin inclusions are features of multiple myeloma, not Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia.
explanation_incorrect.B: Myeloblasts with Auer rods are diagnostic of acute myelogenous leukemia, a myeloid neoplasm rather than a lymphoplasmacytic one.
explanation_incorrect.D: Fewer than 10% polytypic plasma cells with no symptoms describes a reactive or MGUS-like marrow, not macroglobulinemia.
explanation_incorrect.E: Hairlike projections with marrow fibrosis and a dry tap are characteristic of hairy cell leukemia.

educationalObjective: Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia shows lymphoplasmacytic marrow infiltrates with intranuclear IgM inclusions, unlike the cytoplasmic inclusions of myeloma.
source: Generated from 10. Oncology.pdf - Pathology: Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia

subject: Oncology and Hematology
vignette: A 72-year-old woman has anemia, an IgM M spike of 3.5 g/dL, mild lymphadenopathy, and headaches. Skeletal survey shows no lytic lesions; serum calcium and creatinine are normal. She wants to know why this is not multiple myeloma.
question: Which of the following features most strongly favors Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia over multiple myeloma?

options.text: Presence of a monoclonal M spike on serum protein electrophoresis
Hyperviscosity symptoms with an IgM paraprotein and absence of lytic bone lesions
Anemia with normocytic, normochromic red cell indices
Rouleaux formation on peripheral blood smear
Increased urinary Bence Jones light chains

explanation_correct: An IgM paraprotein producing hyperviscosity, together with adenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly but no lytic lesions or CRAB findings, is the signature of Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia. IgM is the largest immunoglobulin, so it drives viscosity-related headache, bleeding, and visual symptoms. Myeloma instead produces IgG or IgA with osteolytic lesions and hypercalcemia.

explanation_incorrect.A: An M spike occurs in both disorders, so its presence alone does not discriminate between them.
explanation_incorrect.C: Anemia is common in both myeloma and Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia and is not a distinguishing feature.
explanation_incorrect.D: Rouleaux formation can occur with any monoclonal paraproteinemia and is not specific for either diagnosis.
explanation_incorrect.E: Bence Jones light-chain proteinuria is characteristic of multiple myeloma; Waldenstrom secretes intact IgM pentamers.

educationalObjective: IgM hyperviscosity without lytic lesions distinguishes Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia from IgG/IgA multiple myeloma.
